title: What is accrual accounting?
subtitle: Recognised by economic obligation, not by cash flow
openingQuestion: Under accrual accounting, when is December's salary expense recognised?
openingOptions: When the labour contract is signed
When salary is paid in January of the following year
In December, when the employee did the work
explanation: Accrual accounting recognises revenue and expenses at the point the economic obligation arises, not when cash moves. December's salary paid in January is still an expense of December, and the unpaid portion sits on the balance sheet as a payable. The goal is for each period's profit to reflect that period's actual activity - the cost is that profit no longer means the same thing as cash.

diagram.label: An economic obligation arises during the period
Revenue and expense are recognised right then
Expense is matched with the revenue it generates
The gap versus real cash sits in receivables and payables

realWorldExample.description: All companies listed in Vietnam are required to apply accrual accounting under Vietnamese Accounting Standards (VAS) when preparing financial statements published to the public and to regulators.

quiz.question: Accrual Accounting recognises:
options: When cash actually moves into or out of the till
When the tax authority confirms the period's figures
When the obligation arises, regardless of cash
When the contract is signed by both parties
quiz.explanation: A credit sale → revenue is recognised right away. A prepayment → expense is allocated month by month.

quiz.question: The income statement and balance sheet use:
options: Whichever method a company chooses to use itself
A mix of both accrual and cash basis
Cash basis, for simplicity and ease of understanding
Accrual, as required by GAAP/IFRS
quiz.explanation: Under GAAP/IFRS → the income statement and balance sheet are fully accrual-based.

quiz.question: The advantage of accrual is:
options: It reflects the true substance of business activity
It lets a company defer taxable income into a later period
It's simpler and costs less in accounting effort
It tells you exactly how much cash is on hand
quiz.explanation: Accrual gives investors and creditors an accurate view of operations.

quiz.question: A drawback of Cash Accounting is:
options: It isn't accepted by any tax authority anywhere in the world
It doesn't reflect the true substance of the business
It's too complex for small-scale businesses
It doesn't show the actual cash balance
quiz.explanation: Example: delaying an invoice into next month → manipulating profit.

quiz.question: A startup shows 100 million profit (accrual) but -50 million (cash). Why?
options: The accountant made an error in one of the two ledgers
This situation cannot happen in reality
Revenue not yet collected, plus large CapEx
The company is hiding a real loss
quiz.explanation: Accrual = 100 (accrued revenue + non-cash expenses). Cash = -50 (CapEx, cash not yet in).

quiz.question: GAAP/IFRS require accrual because:
options: It's simpler, so accountants make fewer mistakes
It helps the tax authority collect more tax
It's a longstanding convention that regulators could drop at any time without consequence
It reflects true activity so investors can compare companies
quiz.explanation: Governments and investors need accurate data → accrual is the global standard.

quiz.question: Should an investor read the income statement or the cash flow statement?
options: Both: the income statement for profit/loss, the cash flow statement for real cash
Only the balance sheet, since it sums up both
Only the cash flow statement, since cash doesn't lie
Only the income statement, since it's the one figure everyone else, including auditors, relies on
quiz.explanation: The income statement ≠ the cash flow statement. You need both to avoid being misled.

keyTakeaways: Accrual: recognised by economic obligation, not by cash
The matching principle: revenue and expense line up in the same period
Most large businesses are required to use accrual

practicePrompt.question: A consulting company completes a project for a client in December and issues a 200-million invoice, but the client only pays in February of the following year. Under accrual accounting, when is this 200-million revenue recognised?
options: In February of the following year - exactly when the company actually receives the cash into its bank account
Recognise it in December, when the company had finished the obligation, even though the cash itself had not arrived
Split evenly: 100 million in December and 100 million in February of the following year
This revenue isn't recognised until there is independent audit confirmation
practicePrompt.explanation: Accrual accounting recognises by economic obligation, not by cash: the company completed its side of the deal (project finished, invoice issued) in December, so the revenue is recognised right in that month, even though the cash only actually lands in the account in February of the following year.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Find an 'accrued liability' in everyday life
application.message: Think of an obligation you've already incurred but haven't paid for yet (this month's staff salary paid next month, an electricity bill used but not yet due) and write it out following accrual logic.
application.secondary: Recognising items like this helps you forecast your cash needs more accurately.

sections.text: Accrual Accounting is the foundation of every modern financial statement - its core principle is recognising revenue and expenses when they arise economically, not when cash actually moves.
The matching principle - the heart of accrual

The matching principle requires that expenses be recognised in the same period as the revenue they generate. **Example:** December's salary expense must be recognised in December - because employees worked and created value that month - even though the company actually pays the salary at the start of January. This unpaid amount creates a line item called 'accrued liabilities' on the balance sheet.

The same applies to revenue: if a consulting company finishes a project in March but the client pays in May, the revenue is still recognised in March - because the service is complete, the economic obligation has arisen. The uncollected amount creates Accounts Receivable on the balance sheet, not a 'non-existent' item.

items: Accrued expenses: expenses already incurred but not yet paid in cash (salaries, interest, taxes)
Accrued revenue: revenue already earned but cash not yet collected (service already completed, invoice not yet issued)
Prepaid expenses: cash already paid but the expense hasn't fully arisen yet (a full year's insurance paid upfront)

sections.label: Why accounting standards require accrual
sections.text: IFRS and VAS both require listed businesses to use accrual accounting because it truly reflects a business's actual operating performance in a period, letting investors fairly compare performance across periods and across companies - instead of being distorted by the random timing of cash in/out.

concepts.def: Recognises revenue/expenses when the economic obligation arises, not by cash flow
Related revenue and expenses must be recognised in the same accounting period
Expenses already incurred but not yet paid in cash
Cash already paid upfront, with the expense allocated gradually over later periods

lines: Accrual accounting separates accounting profit from actual cash flow - which is why you need to read both the income statement and the cash flow statement.
The matching principle is the key to understanding why a payment or receipt shows up in one particular period rather than another.
Nearly every listed business worldwide is required to apply accrual accounting.
